display.title: A Gimmel Tammuz Gift for the Rebbe: The King in the Forest
display.summary_short: Why a small hachlata is a great gift for the Rebbe, told through a boy's birthday letter and a parable of a lost king, a poor man's hut and a box of stale bread.
display.summary_long: The storyteller begins with a story from the Rebbe's room on Yud-Aleph Nissan: of all the reports of new Chabad houses and shuls, the letter that made the Rebbe smile came from a young boy who resolved to wake up five minutes earlier to say the morning brachos from a siddur. He suggests other small hachlatos, such as thinking for a moment before each brachah, or the five things to do before going to sleep: Shema, preparing negel vasser, kissing the mezuzah, and sleeping with a yarmulke and kosher tzitzis. Then, telling listeners it is a parable, he relates how a king lost in a freezing forest is taken in by poor Chaim, who gives him all he has: stale bread, warm water and a sack of straw. The grateful king rewards him with gold, and Chaim builds a house for guests. A neighbor brings the king the same bread, water and straw in a box, and the king gently explains why it is not the same. The lesson: in the darkness of golus, every small mitzvah is precious to Hashem.
display.lesson: Even a small good resolution is a great gift. In the darkness of golus, every brachah said with care and every small mitzvah is precious to Hashem, and brings Moshiach.
